title: Felix and the Harbor
premise: Freya Okonkwo has spent ten years answering anonymous letters left in her bookshop's lending drawer, falling in love with a voice she never met — until the letters stop and Felix Marsh, a disgraced former prosecutor turned harbor-town newcomer, moves in next door. As Freya discovers Felix was the letter writer, she also learns he came to Harbor's End to expose the vineyard empire that destroyed his career and her late husband's name. Torn between the loyalty she owes her daughter's memory of her father and the truth Felix carries, Freya must finally speak the confession she has rehearsed for a decade: that she knew who wrote the letters all along. On the morning of the vineyard's first harvest, with the exposé published and the town divided, Freya chooses truth over duty — and Felix chooses to stay.
about_author: D. M. Quintana is the pen name of a former small-town bookseller who spent years slipping handwritten notes into returned library books before turning to fiction. They write love stories about people who say the hard thing one decade too late — and one harvest too soon.

chapters.title: The Lending Drawer
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Ten years of anonymous letters in the bookshop's lending drawer have ended abruptly, and Freya pretends not to grieve while running the shop and raising her daughter Amara alone. A moving truck arrives next door. Emotional beat: quiet loss disguised as routine, and the first tremor of change.

chapters.title: The Man Next Door
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Felix unpacks boxes of case files he swore he'd burned, watching the bookshop light across the fence. He recognizes Freya from a single photograph kept for ten years but cannot bring himself to introduce himself. Emotional beat: guilt wearing the mask of a fresh start.

chapters.title: Spine Creases
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Felix comes into the shop; their banter is instant and dangerous. He buys a book she once quoted in a letter, and she nearly says so aloud. Amara takes an immediate liking to him, which frightens Freya more than the attraction does. Emotional beat: recognition without permission.

chapters.title: What the Vineyard Owns
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Felix reveals fragments of why he came: the Calloway vineyard empire buried evidence that ruined his career and framed a dockworker — Freya's late husband, Emeka. He asks her, as a bookseller, what the town reads about the Calloways. Emotional beat: duty rekindling into obsession.

chapters.title: Letters, Past Tense
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Freya finds an old letter draft in a donated book — Felix's handwriting. She confronts him at the fence line; he admits nothing, and she says nothing either, both protecting secrets like glass. Emotional beat: two people lying by omission in perfect sync.

chapters.title: Harvest Season
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. The Calloway harvest gala approaches; Felix infiltrates it using Freya's knowledge of the town's social geography. Freya attends on his arm, playing a role that feels less like acting every hour. Emotional beat: intimacy deepening inside a shared deception.

chapters.title: Amara's Question
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Amara, researching her father for a school project, asks Freya whether Emeka was really guilty. Freya's rehearsed answer fails for the first time. She realizes protecting the memory may mean betraying the truth. Emotional beat: motherhood colliding with the lie she's lived.

chapters.title: The Rehearsed Sentence
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Felix publishes the exposé; the town erupts, and Freya's shop becomes a battleground of loyalists and skeptics. When Felix learns Freya knew he was the letter writer for months and stayed silent, he feels the decade invert. Emotional beat: betrayal discovered inside devotion.

chapters.title: First Harvest
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. On the morning the vineyard's first honest harvest comes in, Freya crosses the fence and speaks the sentence she rehearsed for ten years: she always knew it was him, and she loved him through the drawer anyway. Felix must decide whether truth arrived too late. Emotional beat: the climax — confession as surrender and claim.

chapters.title: What Stays
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The town begins reckoning with the truth; Emeka's name is cleared posthumously, and Amara reads her father's real story aloud in the shop. Felix stays, and the lending drawer gets a new sign: no longer anonymous. Emotional beat: resolution — love chosen in full daylight, past tense made present.
